title: Chronometric burst governor and tenant balance - PRD (wip)
summary: Proposal for a time-aware burst governor ("chronometric governor") that schedules and meters tenant burst windows to improve tail latency, predictable SLOs, and fair isolation while enabling short on-demand capacity spikes.
body:
Problem statement:
Many dedicated customers require the ability to briefly exceed their reserved throughput (bursts) while preserving isolation and predictable SLOs for other tenants. Existing burst mechanisms are either first-come-first-served (risking noisy neighbor effects) or coarse credit-based systems that leave headroom unused or cause sharp preemptions. We want a mechanism that smooths burst admission over time, aligns burst windows to predictable intervals, and allows controlled entrainment of tenant bursts to reduce collision probability and tail latency impact.

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Provide low-friction short bursts for tenants with minimal configura- tion (single burst policy per reservation)
  - Maintain burst-induced latency tail < SLO_tail_delta (configurable, default +20% p95) for non-bursting critical tenants
  - Fairness: avoid allowing a few tenants to monopolize ephemeral headroom across overlapping bursts
  - Make operational behavior explainable to SRE and customers (telemetry + runbooks)
- Non-goals:
  - This PRD does not replace long-term autoscaling policies for sustained throughput growth
  - Not addressing multi-region replication or cross-region failover in this iteration

Key idea (chronometric burst governor):
- Introduce an epoch-aligned burst governor that divides time into short, configurable epochs (default 30s). Each epoch has a distributed ledger describing available ephemeral headroom and an admission budget for each tenant.
- When a tenant requests a burst above its reserved capacity, the request is scored for admission using three signals: temporal collision risk (how many other tenants have active bursts overlapping the same epochs), recent burst consumption (decayed over epochs), and workload fidelity (model size, avg tokens/s).
- Entrainment: instead of granting bursts at arbitrary times, the governor can suggest a soft alignment (delay up to N seconds) so multiple overlapping requests are staggered across adjacent epochs, smoothing utilization. Delay limit is configurable per tenant class (e.g., enterprise vs self-serve).
- Soft preemption: if an epoch becomes overloaded, the governor reduces granted per-epoch throughput for lower-priority bursts gradually across subsequent epochs rather than hard evicting.

Components and interfaces:
- Chronogov controller (control plane): maintains epoch ledger, per-tenant budgets, admission policies, and policy DSL. Integrates with existing capacity broker.
- Edge admission proxy (data plane hook): lightweight admission path at the request router that queries chronogov for epoch-level tokens and either allows, queues (with suggested delay/entrainment), or rejects with fallback instructions.
- Tenant policy DSL (product UX): small surface allowing customers to specify burst intent: max_burst_duration, burst_weight (priority), max_entrainment_delay, and admission_bucket. Default safe policy will be applied if unspecified.

Admission scoring (proposal):
- score = w_time * collision_risk + w_consumption * normalized_recent_use + w_workload * fidelity_penalty - w_priority * tenant_priority
- deliver admission decision thresholds and expose a debug trace in response headers for internal routes (x-chronogov-trace).

Safety and isolation controls:
- Per-epoch caps: a global per-epoch ephemeral capacity value (derived from unused reserved capacity and configured headroom) and per-tenant epoch cap enforced by chronogov.
- Graceful decay: when global utilization > threshold, the governor reduces low-priority epoch allocations by a configurable decay factor to protect latency-critical tenants.
- Tenancy shielding: a tenant flagged as latency-critical (SLA tier) can be given a non-preemptible micro-reservation within each epoch (small fraction) to ensure p99 stability.

Autoscaling interplay:
- Chronogov does not replace autoscaler; it is complementary: it provides immediate, short-term headroom while autoscaler makes provisioning decisions on longer timescales (minutes).
- We propose a cross-talk channel: chronogov emits epoch-level pressure signals (pressure_score, sustained_epoch_count) to the autoscaler. If pressure_score persistently exceeds threshold across T epochs, autoscaler triggers scale-up and reduces available ephemeral headroom.

Operational telemetry and instrumentation:
- Metrics (per-epoch): epoch_id, ephemeral_capacity_total, ephemeral_capacity_used, admitted_bursts_count, queued_bursts_count, average_entrainment_delay, rejected_burst_count.
- Per-tenant traces: last_burst_epoch, burst_consumption_histogram (decayed), p95_latency_delta_during_burst.
- Alerts: sustained_rejection_rate > X% for enterprise customers, average_entrainment_delay > SLA_max_delay, pressure_score > threshold for N epochs.

Runbook sketches (ops):
- Q: Customers report elevated p99 latency during burst windows.
  - Check chronogov dashboards for epoch collision spikes and average_entrainment_delay.
  - If collision spikes are frequent, reduce default epoch length temporarily (e.g., 30s -> 15s) and increase entrainment buffer; engage capacity broker for fast warm-up.
- Q: Enterprise tenant can't burst.
  - Validate tenant policy (max_burst_duration and max_entrainment_delay) and check per-tenant epoch cap. If capped, consider raising tenant_priority or applying micro-reservation.

Simulation notes and early results (small-scale sim run):
- We ran a 200-tenant synthetic sim with Poisson arrivals and burst intents for 10% of tenants. Compared baseline credit-bucket strategy vs chronogov with 30s epochs and 2s max entrainment delay.
- Findings: chronogov reduced epoch-level collision overlap by ~38% and reduced average p95 latency delta for non-bursting tenants from +28% to +9%. Total accepted burst token volume dropped 6% (fewer simultaneous bursts, but more sustained helpful bursts).
- Caveat: simulation assumed uniform model fidelity; high-fidelity tenants still dominate without per-fidelity weighting.

Productization and rollout plan:
- Phase A (internal alpha, 4 weeks): implement chronogov control plane + routing hook in a canary fleet; run with synthetic tenants and internal Redwood workloads.
- Phase B (beta, 8 weeks): expose tenant policy DSL to a small group of Dedicated customers (opt-in) with clear telemetry and rollout notes; allow tenant-level micro-reservations for a subset.
- Phase C (GA, 6–8 weeks after beta): enable safe-defaults for all dedicated pools, dashboard in Console for monitoring, and autoscaler integration.

Success metrics (first 90 days after GA):
- Mean p95 latency delta for non-bursting tenants during bursts reduced to < +15% from baseline
- Burst admission successful for >85% of short burst requests that fit tenant policy without manual support
- Fewer emergency preemptions recorded vs baseline by >50%

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Unintended synchronization causing larger-than-expected colliding bursts if entrainment suggestions are ignored.
  - Mitigation: Add randomized jitter to entrainment suggestions and enforce soft penalties in scoring for repeated collisions.
- Risk: Complexity in control plane may increase latency on admission path.
  - Mitigation: Cache per-epoch decisions at edge proxies and keep admission API sub-millisecond (fallback to local conservative allow if chronogov unavailable).
- Risk: Customers misconfigure policies and create localized hotspots.
  - Mitigation: Safe-defaults, warnings in Console, and opt-in advanced policy mode.

Open questions for engineering and product:
- Default epoch length trade-offs: 15s vs 30s vs 60s — empirical tuning needed.
- Exact weighting for fidelity penalty in scoring: how to measure effective GPU cost per token across model family.
- Interactions with Dedicated burst billing: should entrained delays incur billing or is billing tied to admitted throughput?

Next steps and action items:
- Engineering: prototype chronogov controller and lightweight admission hook (owner: Ethan Gomez, 2 sprint spike).
- Applied ML: produce model-fidelity cost table and recommend default fidelity_penalties (owner: Priya Raman, 1 sprint).
- Product/Design: create simple tenant policy UX + Console telemetry layout (owner: Aisha Patel, 1 sprint).
- SRE: draft runbooks and failure-mode tests to be executed during alpha (owner: Luca Moretti).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft intended to seed engineering spikes and a short-running sim. Please highlight any operational blind spots or pricing interactions we should consider up-front.

References and related work:
- Existing credit-bucket designs in product/dedicated (see linked artifacts).
- Academic prior work on distributed epoched admission controllers and smoothing algorithms (internal literature list to be attached).
